row.basis: heart-prayer; moving lips; unheard voice
row.note: The commentary joins remembrance on the tongue and in the heart; Hannah prays in her heart, with moving lips but an unheard voice, making an unusually close scriptural scene of inward yet bodily prayer.

row.basis: Hannah's lips and unheard voice
row.note: Berakhot derives prayer rules from Hannah's verse: direct the heart, move the lips, and do not make the voice heard. It gives the commentary's loud/quiet prayer contrast a precise rabbinic liturgical reading.

row.basis: quiet prayer; God hears the heart
row.note: Cyprian teaches that prayer should be quiet because God hears the heart rather than the volume of a voice. This directly interprets the commentary's claim that God knows recitation whether it is on the tongue or in the heart.

row.basis: secret prayer; Father sees in secret
row.note: The commentary pairs inward prayer with God's knowledge of what is concealed; Jesus commands prayer in the shut room, where the Father sees in secret, giving that pair a Christian discipline of prayer.

row.basis: God searches hearts; Spirit's intention
row.note: The commentary says the Lord knows worship that remains inside; Romans names God as the searcher of hearts who knows the Spirit's intention, making divine knowledge the ground of unvoiced intercession.

row.basis: Jesus knows reasoning within hearts
row.note: The commentary's God knows what is hidden as well as what is uttered; Mark's Jesus immediately knows the scribes' inward reasoning, a narrative Christian counterpart focused on concealed thought.

row.basis: word on tongue already known
row.note: The commentary explicitly sets raised speech beside what remains hidden. Psalm 139 says that before a word is on the tongue, YHWH knows it completely, giving the verbal side of that claim its closest Hebrew formulation.

row.basis: God observes heart and hears tongue
row.note: The commentary distinguishes heart and tongue while affirming God's knowledge of both. Wisdom calls God an observer of the heart and a hearer of the tongue, preserving both terms in one ethical warning about speech.

row.basis: no thought or word hidden
row.note: The commentary joins disclosed speech to what stays concealed; Sirach says that no thought escapes God and no word is hidden from him, supplying a compact Jewish formulation of both halves.

row.basis: secret things and revealed things
row.note: The commentary treats hidden and open things as known by God and brought into relation with recited teaching. Deuteronomy assigns secret things to YHWH and revealed things to Israel for doing the Torah, sharpening the disclosure boundary.

row.basis: God reveals deep and hidden things
row.note: The commentary turns concealment into emergence and says God knows the hidden. Daniel's God reveals deep and hidden things, knows what is in darkness, and has light with him, matching both disclosure and light-darkness imagery.

row.basis: outward appearance and heart
row.note: The commentary contrasts what is open with inward reality. In Samuel, humans look at outward appearance while YHWH looks at the heart, a concrete distinction between visible surface and divinely known interior.

row.basis: YHWH searches heart and tests inward self
row.note: The commentary says the hidden interior is known even when no voice exposes it. Jeremiah presents YHWH as searching the heart and testing the inward person, placing that claim in judgment language.

row.basis: deep things from darkness brought to light
row.note: The commentary's second scene makes the concealed come out from its cover. Job says God uncovers deep things from darkness and brings deep shadow into light, a direct divine movement from hiddenness to exposure.

row.basis: hidden thing brought to light
row.note: The commentary uses physical emergence and a cleared well to picture disclosure. Job's mining poem says that a hidden thing is brought to light, supplying a terrestrial extraction image without making the human miner identical with God.

row.basis: no creature hidden; all exposed to God
row.note: The commentary's open/hidden pair is made absolute here: Hebrews says no creature is hidden before God and all stand exposed to his eyes, extending the claim beyond speech to every creature.

row.basis: hidden darkness and counsels of hearts disclosed
row.note: The commentary joins concealed things emerging from cover with the knowledge of inner reality. Paul says the Lord will bring hidden darkness to light and disclose the counsels of hearts, uniting both movements in judgment.

row.basis: hidden made manifest; secret made known
row.note: The commentary describes concealment as capable of becoming visible. Jesus states that nothing hidden will fail to become manifest and no secret will fail to become known and come to light, a close disclosure formula.

row.basis: YHWH reveals secret to prophets
row.note: The commentary frames recited divine speech around what God knows in secret. Amos says the Lord reveals his secret to prophetic servants, adding a biblical account of hidden counsel becoming prophetic proclamation.

row.basis: mystery hidden through ages now manifested
row.note: The commentary makes the hidden something God can bring out. Colossians calls Christ's mystery hidden through ages and generations but now manifested to the saints, a Christian revelation-history form of that movement.

row.basis: written song taught and put in mouths
row.note: The commentary reads 87:6 as recitation from memory or from a text. Deuteronomy orders a song to be written, taught, and put in Israel's mouths, explicitly joining writing, learning, and oral recitation.

row.basis: song not forgotten from descendants' mouths
row.note: The commentary foregrounds the promise of recitation without forgetting. Deuteronomy says the taught song will not be forgotten from descendants' mouths, a close covenantal counterpart to preserved oral memory.

row.basis: Torah book in mouth and meditation
row.note: The commentary joins an uttered reading to an inward one. Joshua requires the Torah book not to depart from the mouth and commands meditation on it day and night, holding oral and interior engagement together.

row.basis: word stored in heart
row.note: The commentary calls recitation possible from the heart. The psalmist says the divine word has been stored or hidden in the heart, turning inward retention into a safeguard for faithful action.

row.basis: word in mouth and heart
row.note: The commentary's central pair is stated almost structurally here: Deuteronomy says the word is very near, in the mouth and in the heart, so that it can be done.

row.basis: word in mouth and heart
row.note: The commentary says the taught word is known whether voiced or held within. Romans reuses the mouth-and-heart formula for the proclaimed word of faith, giving the paired locations a Christ-centered reading.

row.basis: law placed in mind and written on heart
row.note: The commentary's recitation from the heart is not merely silent sound. Hebrews describes God's law placed in minds and written on hearts, a durable inward inscription of revealed teaching.

row.basis: word dwelling richly; songs in hearts
row.note: The commentary connects recitation, remembrance, and worship in tongue and heart. Colossians commands Christ's word to dwell richly and joins teaching with sung worship in hearts, preserving that combined practice.

row.basis: spoken psalms and melody in heart
row.note: The commentary distinguishes audible speech from inward remembrance without separating them. Ephesians pairs speaking psalms and hymns with singing and making melody in the heart to the Lord.

row.basis: one reads aloud and others hear
row.note: The commentary begins with the voice of recitation. Revelation blesses the single reader who reads prophecy aloud together with those who hear it, a specific early Christian scene of voiced scripture.

row.basis: God's words remain in successive mouths
row.note: The commentary treats divine teaching as recited and not forgotten. Isaiah's covenant says God's words will not depart from the prophet's mouth or the mouths of descendants, extending memorized speech through generations.

row.basis: Arabic q-r-' label; Hebrew qara' reading
row.note: The commentary labels the 87:6 reading root q-r-'. Deuteronomy uses the Hebrew cognate qara' for reading the Torah before all Israel in their hearing, showing a Semitic root in an explicitly public reading act.

row.basis: Arabic dhikr label; Hebrew zkr and God's name
row.note: The commentary labels 87:15 with dhikr and has the worshipper remember the Lord's name. Psalm 20 uses Hebrew zkr for Israel's making mention of YHWH's name, a close cognate-and-ritual match.

row.basis: Arabic dhikr label; Hebrew zikri and divine name
row.note: The commentary's dhikr label joins remembrance to the Lord's name. Exodus calls YHWH's declared name his zikri, "my memorial/remembrance," making name and remembrance inseparable in divine self-disclosure.

row.basis: Hebrew zkr, book of remembrance, and honored name
row.note: The commentary's dhikr of the Lord's name is voiced worship. Malachi has God hear those who speak together and honor his name, then records them in a book of remembrance from Hebrew zkr.

row.basis: calling on the Lord's name
row.note: The commentary ends the sequence with remembering the Lord's name and praying. Romans applies the scriptural promise that everyone who calls on the Lord's name will be saved, making invocation of the name a Christian prayer act.

row.basis: rain makes earth bring forth and sprout
row.note: The commentary says rain draws pasture from soil. Isaiah compares rain and snow that water the earth and make it bring forth and sprout, a close image of divinely enabled vegetal emergence.

row.basis: rainless wasteland satisfied; grass sprouts
row.note: The commentary moves from rain and earth to grass coming out. In God's questions to Job, the desolate ground is satisfied so that grass is caused to sprout, placing pasture-growth under divine agency.

row.basis: God makes grass grow from earth
row.note: The commentary links 87:4's bringing out of pasture to divine action. Psalm 104 says God makes grass grow for cattle and vegetation for human service, a direct hymn-like counterpart to that pastoral image.

row.basis: bright sky-light cannot be seen
row.note: The commentary adds the paradox that excessive sunlight can obstruct sight. Job says people cannot see the bright light in the skies, giving a specific biblical instance where brightness defeats vision.

row.basis: unable to see because of brilliant light
row.note: The commentary's cehra image is an eye unable to see in sun. Paul says he could not see because of the brilliance of the heavenly light, a narrative instance of sight overwhelmed by light.

row.basis: Shema audible to one's own ear
row.note: The commentary places elevated and inward recitation together. This Mishnah debates whether a Shema made audible to the reciter's own ear fulfills the duty, giving low but articulated sound a specific legal significance.

row.basis: wordless groanings in prayer
row.note: The commentary allows worship to remain within rather than rise as loud speech. Romans describes the Spirit's intercession through groanings too deep for words, an explicit Christian image of prayer beyond utterance.

row.basis: communal silence and speech to self and God
row.note: The commentary balances voiced and internal devotion. Paul tells an uninterpreted speaker to keep silence in the assembly while speaking to himself and to God, distinguishing public sound from God-directed speech.

row.basis: God knows needs before spoken prayer
row.note: The commentary says God knows an inward as well as uttered reading. Augustine explains that prayer-words do not inform God, who already knows human need, but exercise the pray-er’s desire; this is a patristic account of the same premise.

row.basis: seed sprouts and grows without the sower's knowing
row.note: The commentary makes hiddenness a process of emergence, especially grass from earth. Jesus' seed sprouts and grows while the sower does not know how, setting hidden vegetal growth beside the commentary's divine knowing.

row.basis: opened eyes and a seen well of water
row.note: The commentary uses a cleared, visible well as an image of disclosure. God opens Hagar's eyes and she sees a well of water, making hidden provision visible without claiming that the well itself was newly created.

row.basis: covered under wings and feathers
row.note: The commentary's hawafi are feathers hidden below the leading wing-feathers. Psalm 91 pictures protection under God's wings and feathers, offering a concrete feather-cover image while giving it a protective sense.

row.basis: chicks gathered under a bird's wings
row.note: The commentary uses concealed lesser feathers beneath a wing. Jesus' hen image gathers chicks under wings, another bird-cover scene whose protective purpose adds a relational use of the concealed space.

row.basis: shining face covered by a veil
row.note: The commentary says excess light can itself become a covering. Exodus combines Moses' shining face with his putting on a veil, a biblical scene in which radiance and covering are deliberately held together.

row.basis: fire followed by a sound of thin silence
row.note: The commentary connects volume, concealment, and the Qur'anic approach to Moses' fire. After fire, Elijah's Horeb scene contains qol demamah daqqah, a "sound of thin silence," an indirect but unusually apt acoustic counter-image.

row.basis: Moses and fire in the bush
row.note: The commentary locates the Qur'anic loud/hidden saying immediately before Moses sees fire. Exodus likewise gives Moses a fire-theophany, though specifically a bush burning without being consumed, so the shared scene and its differing detail can be compared.

row.basis: God calls Moses from the bush
row.note: The commentary's nearby Qur'anic setting moves from divine knowledge of speech to the Moses-fire encounter. Exodus 3:4 contributes the verbal side within its own verse: God calls Moses by name from the bush.

row.basis: revealed words placed on the heart
row.note: The commentary says the taught word may be held in the heart as well as voiced. Deuteronomy commands that the words given that day be upon Israel's heart, making inward retention the first response to revelation.

row.basis: repeated words spoken through daily life
row.note: The commentary treats recitation as an active oral practice. Deuteronomy tells Israel to repeat the words to children and speak of them at home, on the road, at bedtime, and on rising, giving memorized teaching a daily voice.

row.basis: teaching kept within and ready on lips
row.note: The commentary's tongue-and-heart recitation has a close wisdom counterpart: Proverbs calls it pleasant to keep teachings within oneself when they are all ready upon one's lips.

row.basis: Torah within and written on heart
row.note: The commentary's inward reading is more than quiet sound. Jeremiah's new-covenant promise places the Torah within the people and writes it on their hearts, a strong Hebrew Bible image of internalized revelation.

row.basis: Arabic q-r-' label; Hebrew qara' book-reading
row.note: The commentary labels 87:6 with q-r-'. Nehemiah uses Hebrew qara' for reading aloud from the Torah book and adds interpretation so that listeners understand, linking cognate reading to voiced instruction and comprehension.

row.basis: audible Scripture reading and understanding
row.note: The commentary joins recitation with being aware of what is said. Philip hears the Ethiopian reading and asks whether he understands what he reads, a concrete Christian scene of oral scripture and understanding.

row.basis: Spirit-written letter on human hearts
row.note: The commentary contrasts a text looked at with one retained in the heart. Paul calls the Corinthians Christ's letter, written by the Spirit on human hearts rather than with ink, making inward inscription a reading-image.

row.basis: Spirit teaches and brings Jesus' words to remembrance
row.note: The commentary reads 87:6 as divinely enabled recitation that does not forget. Jesus promises that the Spirit will teach and remind the disciples of his words, a direct Christian account of preserved taught speech.

row.basis: speak in hearts and be silent
row.note: The commentary's first scene holds lowered voice beside interior speech. This psalm commands hearers to speak in their hearts upon their beds and be silent, a compact Hebrew pairing of inward utterance and silence.

row.basis: lips honor God while heart is distant
row.note: The commentary permits remembrance with tongue and heart together. Isaiah critiques honor rendered with lips while the heart remains far away, adding the ethical test that exterior speech cannot replace inward attachment.

row.basis: lips and distant heart
row.note: The commentary's two locations of worship are tested by Jesus' citation: these people honor God with lips while their heart is far from him. Its Christian use makes the tongue-heart relation a question of genuine worship.

row.basis: prayer and song with spirit and mind
row.note: The commentary distinguishes raised sound from an inward mode of worship. Paul resolves a comparable pairing by praying and singing with both spirit and mind, bringing cognition into voiced prayer and song.

row.basis: calling on YHWH's name
row.note: The commentary closes with remembering the Lord's name and prayer. Genesis describes people beginning to call on YHWH's name, an early biblical scene in which the divine name is invoked in worship.

row.basis: Hebrew zkr: God causes his name to be remembered
row.note: The commentary's dhikr label links remembrance to the Lord's name. At the altar, YHWH promises to come where he causes his name to be remembered, using Hebrew zkr in a specifically cultic setting.

row.basis: Hebrew zekher, name, and desire of the soul
row.note: The commentary's dhikr is possible in the heart as well as on the tongue. Isaiah joins God's name and zekher, "memorial/remembrance," to the desire of the soul, an inward cognate counterpart.

row.basis: YHWH exposes Sarah's inward laughter
row.note: The commentary says God knows what is not openly voiced. YHWH questions Sarah's private laughter and its inner reasoning, giving a narrative instance in which concealed thought is directly known.

row.basis: prayer spoken in the heart
row.note: The commentary allows divine address to remain inward. Abraham's servant says he had not finished speaking in his heart when Rebekah appeared, a prayer narrative that makes interior speech consequential before God.

row.basis: God alone knows every human heart
row.note: The commentary joins prayer to divine knowledge of the hidden. Solomon asks God to hear from heaven because God alone knows the heart of every person, making omniscience part of temple prayer.

row.basis: deep counsel in the heart drawn out
row.note: The commentary says a hidden thing can be extracted and illustrates it with water and a well. Proverbs likens purpose in a person's heart to deep water that one of understanding draws out, joining inner concealment and extraction.

row.basis: body made in secret not hidden from God
row.note: The commentary moves from what is hidden to what God knows and brings into view. This psalm says a body made in secret in earth-like depths was not hidden from God, extending the claim to concealed organic formation.

row.basis: mouth uttering things hidden from the foundation
row.note: The commentary connects recited speech with the disclosure of what lies hidden. Matthew presents Jesus' parabolic speech as uttering things hidden from the world's foundation, a Christian form of voiced unveiling.

row.basis: prayer to the Lord as knower of all hearts
row.note: The commentary says inward realities are known to God. Before choosing Matthias, the disciples pray to the Lord specifically as the knower of everyone's heart, making the claim part of communal discernment.

row.basis: word judges thoughts and intentions of heart
row.note: The commentary treats the recited word and hidden interior as joined under divine knowledge. Hebrews says God's word discerns thoughts and intentions of the heart, making spoken or written revelation an examiner of what is concealed.

row.basis: secrets of heart disclosed in worship
row.note: The commentary connects hidden knowledge, audible word, and prayer. Paul says an outsider's heart-secrets are disclosed and that person then worships God and declares God's presence, a tightly related congregational scene.

row.basis: rain prepared for earth and grass made to grow
row.note: The commentary explicitly imagines rain drawing pasture from soil. Psalm 147 says God prepares rain for the earth and makes grass sprout on mountains, matching rain, ground, growth, and divine agency in one verse.

row.basis: planting, watering, and God giving growth
row.note: The commentary makes pasture's emergence God's act despite rain and soil. Paul distinguishes human planting and watering from God who gives the growth, a Christian agricultural image of the same agency distinction.

row.basis: voice heard from fire but no form seen
row.note: The commentary locates loud and hidden speech beside Moses' fire and explores visible versus concealed. Deuteronomy says YHWH spoke from fire, Israel heard a sound of words, but saw no form, uniting auditory revelation with visual withholding.

row.basis: fire, dense darkness, and a great voice
row.note: The commentary places loud speech, concealment, and the Moses-fire setting together. In WLC's Hebrew verse numbering, Deuteronomy recounts YHWH's great voice from fire, cloud, and dense darkness, an unusually close cluster of those images.

row.basis: brightness that Israel could not gaze at
row.note: The commentary's secondary image is sight defeated by excessive light. Paul says Israel could not gaze at Moses' face because of its glory, making visual incapacity caused by radiance explicit.

row.basis: unheard voice without speech or words
row.note: The commentary's phonetic scene contrasts audible high speech with what remains unspoken. Psalm 19 says there is no speech or words and no voice is heard, yet its surrounding hymn presents creation as communicating; the parallel is poetic rather than liturgical.

row.basis: few words before God
row.note: The commentary invokes a measured rather than raised prayer-voice. Ecclesiastes warns against hasty speech before God and says that human words should be few, an explicit wisdom restraint on devotional utterance.

row.basis: Moses read while a veil lies on the heart
row.note: The commentary connects reading, heart, and covering. Paul says that when Moses is read a veil lies on the heart, a Christian interpretive image in which scriptural reading itself can remain interiorly covered.

row.basis: mouth opened in parable and ancient dark sayings
row.note: The commentary makes disclosure possible through a spoken word. The psalmist opens his mouth in a parable to utter ancient riddling sayings, a Hebrew example of voiced transmission of what is not immediately plain.

row.basis: liturgical remembrance in enacted worship
row.note: The commentary joins dhikr to prayer. Paul's Eucharistic command, "do this in remembrance of me," makes remembrance a repeated Christian worship-act, though its object and rite differ from remembering God's name in 87:15.

row.basis: keep a king's secret; reveal God's works
row.note: The commentary turns secret and open into a movement of disclosure. Tobit distinguishes keeping a ruler's secret from honoring God by revealing God's deeds, supplying a Jewish ethical rule about concealment and proclamation.

row.basis: earth produces first blade, then ear and grain
row.note: The commentary's pasture comes out of the earth. Jesus describes the earth producing the crop in ordered stages beginning with the blade, a parabolic vegetal emergence whose setting differs from the commentary's rain image.

row.basis: well-mouth stone rolled away for watering
row.note: The commentary gives a cleared well whose water is made visible as an image of disclosure. Genesis describes shepherds rolling the stone from a well's mouth to water sheep and replacing it, a concrete cover-and-uncover water scene.

row.basis: previously hidden things now announced
row.note: The commentary says God may bring the hidden out. Isaiah tells the audience that hidden things they had not known are now announced, a prophetic disclosure formula rather than a physical emergence image.

row.basis: unapproachable light that no human can see
row.note: The commentary says overwhelming light can function like a cover to sight. First Timothy places God in unapproachable light whom no human has seen or can see, a theological extension of visual excess beyond the sun-image.
